sentences.text: Euoplocephalus was a large herbivorous ankylosaurid dinosaur that lived in Canada during the Late Cretaceous period.
This animal reached a length of 5.3 meters and a body mass of 2 metric tons.
It possessed bony armor covering its head and body, excluding parts of the limbs and possibly the tail tip.
The premaxillae, or front snout bones, of Euoplocephalus are not covered by dermal ossifications.
The largest known skull of Euoplocephalus, specimen AMNH 5403, measures 411 millimeters in length and 478 millimeters in width.
Internally, many bones were fused together to support the heavy armor.
It was the first ankylosaurid discovered to have armored eyelids that could close to cover its eyes.
The largest and tallest scutes of Euoplocephalus may have been located on the shoulders, with some reaching a base length of fifteen centimeters.
The nuchal crest of Euoplocephalus was covered by two osteoderms on each side between the squamosal horns.
The armor of Euoplocephalus may have formed a pavement-like structure with transverse bands if configured similarly to the genus Scolosaurus.
The first fossil of Euoplocephalus was discovered in Alberta in 1897 by Lawrence Morris Lambe on August 18, 1897, in the Red Deer River valley near present-day Dinosaur Provincial Park.
The genus was originally named Stereocephalus in 1902 but was renamed Euoplocephalus in 1910 because the original name was already used for an insect.
Edwin Hennig classified Euoplocephalus tutus under the genus Palaeoscincus in 1915.
Euoplocephalus was approximately 5.3 meters long and weighed about 2 metric tons.
Euoplocephalus is thought to have been a herbivore, like other ankylosaurs.
Complex respiratory passages in the skull suggest Euoplocephalus had a good sense of smell.
According to Coombs, Euoplocephalus may have been capable of running at speeds comparable to modern rhinoceroses and hippos.
The discovery of Euoplocephalus as isolated elements or partial skeletons suggests the animal lived solitarily or in small groups.
A 2009 study concluded that large ankylosaurian tail clubs could generate enough force to break bone during impacts.
While tail swinging is feasible in ankylosaurids, it is unknown whether the tail was used for defense against predators, combat between individuals, or both.
The banded arrangement of Euoplocephalus's armor is thought to have allowed for some freedom of movement.
Researchers reconstructed the dinosaur's inner ear and concluded it was capable of hearing low frequencies.
The form and function of the complex air passages and sinuses in the Euoplocephalus snout are not yet completely understood.
It is debated whether the cervical half-rings of Euoplocephalus were fused osteoderms or a lower layer of ossified cartilage, as suggested by Arbour et al. in 2013.

Historically, Euoplocephalus fossils were thought to date from 76.5 to 67 million years ago, spanning the Campanian and Maastrichtian ages, though it lived in North America during the late Cretaceous, approximately 76.5 to 75.4 million years ago.
There is a debate regarding the number of valid Euoplocephalus specimens, with some experts accepting many remains while others limit them to about a dozen.
There is a debate regarding whether the variation in Euoplocephalus skulls represents multiple species or individual variation within a single species.
Recent studies have debated the attribution of fossils, referring Horseshoe Canyon specimens to Anodontosaurus and Two Medicine specimens to Oohkotokia.
